# Locating and Replacing the Camshaft Position Sensor on a 2010 Chevrolet Camaro V6

The error code P0017, specifically "Crankshaft Position - Camshaft position correlation - bank 1 sensor B," points directly to a synchronization issue between the crankshaft and camshaft sensors. On the 3.6L V6 engine found in the 2010 LT model, this is almost invariably caused by a failing camshaft position sensor rather than an electrical wiring fault or timing chain skip, provided the vehicle has not suffered catastrophic timing failure. The physical location of this component is critical for diagnosis and replacement.

The camshaft position sensor on the 3.6L LSX-derived V6 engine is mounted on the passenger side of the engine block (Bank 1), near the front of the motor. It sits close to the exhaust manifold, which creates a specific set of thermal and environmental challenges. Unlike some flat-plane crank engines where sensors are tucked deep behind timing covers, this sensor is accessible but requires careful navigation around the upper intake plenum and the serpentine belt drive accessories.

To access the sensor, you must first remove the engine cover to expose the top of the V6. Once the cover is off, locate the passenger-side valve cover. The sensor itself is not bolted directly to the block in a way that requires removing major components like the alternator or the water pump; however, you will need to loosen the serpentine belt tensioner and slide the belt off the crankshaft pulley. This step is mandatory because the lower part of the sensor housing often interferes with the accessory drive assembly.

When replacing the sensor, do not simply swap it in without checking the connector and wiring harness for chafing or corrosion. A common pitfall on high-mileage vehicles is finding a sensor that tests good at the bench but fails immediately upon installation due to heat soak from the exhaust manifold warping the mounting bracket slightly. The 2010 Camaro's engine bay runs hot, and the plastic connector housing can become brittle over time. If the original connector feels stiff or cracked, replace it along with the sensor. A loose connection here mimics a sensor failure by sending intermittent signals to the Powertrain Control Module (PCM).

After installing the new sensor, ensure the electrical connector clicks firmly into place. The sensor uses a Hall-effect switch mechanism, meaning it relies on magnetic fields and physical clearance to operate correctly. If the sensor is mounted too tightly against the camshaft gear teeth or if there is debris in the mounting bore, the signal will be erratic, triggering the P0017 code again immediately after clearing it.

It is also prudent to inspect the crankshaft position sensor while you are at it. Since the error code indicates a correlation issue, the PCM might be receiving valid data from one but invalid data from the other. If the crank sensor is also showing signs of wear or has a high resistance reading on your multimeter, replace both simultaneously. This prevents a recurrence of the synchronization error and saves you another trip to the garage.

Finally, clear the diagnostic trouble codes with a scan tool and perform a test drive that includes varying RPMs from idle to redline. The engine control unit needs to verify that the cam and crank signals are staying in sync under load. If the light returns after a short drive, re-inspect the wiring harness for rodent damage or check for a vacuum leak on Bank 1, as unburned fuel can sometimes contaminate the sensor tip.
